questions.question_text: Utah is a trust deed state, which means most residential loans use:
questions.correct_answer: A deed of trust instead of a mortgage
distractors: A land contract with seller financing
questions.explanation: Utah lending is dominated by trust deeds under 57-1-19 and following, with a trustee holding power of sale. That is what makes non-judicial foreclosure available.

questions.question_text: What is the most common method of foreclosure in Utah?
distractors: Power of sale through the county
questions.explanation: The trustee's sale under 57-1-23 through 57-1-27 is the usual route: a notice of default is recorded, at least three months pass, and then notice of sale is given. Judicial foreclosure exists but is rarely used.

questions.question_text: After a Notice of Default is recorded in Utah, the borrower has how long to reinstate the loan?
questions.explanation: The trustee may not proceed until at least three months have elapsed from recording the notice of default (57-1-24), and the trustor may cure the default within that period (57-1-31). Notice of sale must then be published once a week for three consecutive weeks, with the last publication 10 to 30 days before the sale, and posted at least 20 days before it.

questions.question_text: After a trustee's sale in Utah, the former owner generally has:
questions.explanation: A non-judicial trustee's sale in Utah carries no statutory redemption period. The lender's remaining recourse is a deficiency action, which 57-1-32 requires to be filed within three months of the sale and caps at the debt less the property's fair market value.

questions.question_text: What is the approximate minimum timeline for a non-judicial foreclosure in Utah from Notice of Default to sale?
questions.explanation: The floor is roughly four months: three months must elapse after the notice of default (57-1-24), and the notice of sale must then be published for three consecutive weeks and posted at least 20 days before the sale (57-1-25).

questions.question_text: Utah's construction lien statute, Title 38, Chapter 1a, allows which parties to lien property?
distractors: Only the property owner's direct contractors
questions.explanation: Title 38, Chapter 1a, Preconstruction and Construction Liens — the successor to Utah's old mechanic's lien act — gives contractors, subcontractors, and suppliers a lien for the reasonable value of their work. Preliminary notice through the State Construction Registry is required to preserve the right.

questions.question_text: Mechanic's lien priority in Utah can date back to:
distractors: The date the lien notice was recorded
The date the construction contract was signed
The date the building permit was issued
questions.explanation: A construction lien relates back to and takes effect as of the time of the first preliminary notice filing, giving it priority over encumbrances that attach after that filing (38-1a-503(1)). Utah's older rule tying priority to commencement of visible work no longer applies.

questions.question_text: A homeowner pays a contractor in full, but the contractor fails to pay a subcontractor. The subcontractor files a mechanic's lien. The homeowner may seek help from:
distractors: The Division of Real Estate only
questions.explanation: The Residence Lien Restriction and Lien Recovery Fund, administered by DOPL under Title 38, Chapter 11, protects an owner-occupant who contracted with a licensed or exempt original contractor and paid in full: 38-11-107 bars the subcontractor's lien once the owner obtains a certificate of compliance, and the fund pays the unpaid subcontractor.

questions.question_text: To preserve mechanic's lien rights in Utah, a subcontractor must:
distractors: Register with the Division of Real Estate
File a claim within 10 days of starting work
questions.explanation: A preliminary notice must be filed with the State Construction Registry no later than 20 days after the claimant first provides construction work (38-1a-501(1)(a)). A late notice covers only work provided five days after it is filed, and has no effect at all if filed more than 10 days after a notice of completion.

questions.question_text: The Residence Lien Restriction and Lien Recovery Fund primarily protects:
questions.correct_answer: Homeowners from paying twice for the same work
questions.explanation: Title 38, Chapter 11 keeps an owner-occupant who already paid a licensed original contractor in full from paying a second time, and compensates the subcontractor from the fund instead of leaving a lien on the residence.

questions.question_text: How many years of continuous possession are required for adverse possession in Utah?
questions.explanation: The land must be occupied and claimed continuously for seven years, and the claimant and predecessors must have paid all taxes levied and assessed on it (78B-2-214).

questions.question_text: In addition to continuous possession for 7 years, Utah's adverse possession requires the claimant to:
questions.correct_answer: Pay property taxes during the entire period
distractors: File notice with the county recorder
Obtain a court order before the period starts
Register with the Division of Real Estate
questions.explanation: Payment of all taxes levied and assessed during the seven-year period is an express element under 78B-2-214, on top of the common-law elements of continuous, open, notorious, hostile, and exclusive possession.

questions.question_text: Under Utah's Statute of Frauds, which agreement must be in writing to be enforceable?
questions.correct_answer: A contract for the sale of real property
distractors: An oral agreement to share a commission
questions.explanation: A contract for the sale of land, or a lease for longer than one year, is void unless it is in writing and signed by the party by whom the sale or lease is to be made (25-5-3). 25-5-4(1)(e) adds that an agreement employing a broker to buy or sell real estate for compensation must also be written.

questions.question_text: A landlord and tenant verbally agree to a 2-year lease. Under the Statute of Frauds, this lease is:
questions.correct_answer: Unenforceable because it exceeds one year
distractors: Valid for the first year only
Enforceable if witnessed by two parties
questions.explanation: A writing is required for any lease for a term longer than one year (25-5-3), so a purely oral two-year lease is unenforceable while a one-year or shorter lease may be oral (25-5-1).

questions.question_text: A person occupies vacant land openly for 6 years, pays all taxes, and uses it exclusively. Can they claim adverse possession?
questions.correct_answer: No, 7 years of possession is required
distractors: Yes, 5 years is sufficient in Utah
Yes, if they file a quiet title action now
No, adverse possession only applies to structures
questions.explanation: Seven continuous years plus payment of all taxes are required (78B-2-214). At six years the statutory period is simply not complete, and a quiet title action filed now would fail.
